Most foolish man that I am, to have left you, father, if an opportunity was given to envy and power to conspirators! For, while I lingered long for your safety, I betrayed my own, and yet I have nothing to impute to myself. You ordered me to depart, father. For you I was abroad, father, lest Syllaeus deceive your old age, strip you of the kingdom while you lived and assail your safety before Caesar. Rome is my witness to family devotion; Caesar too, guardian of the world, censor of all and judge of my heart, was accustomed to call me a lover of my father. Bear witness, Caesar, to what I said of my father before you, before whom alone I could have harmed him. Bear witness for me, I say, you who had pronounced upon others and thought the murder of a father should be investigated, not disregarded. If only your presence would favour me! But you are absent and far away, and without you I am condemned by my father. Yet though absent, you are present in your letters. I offer your writings, which would-be murderers of their fathers usually fear; I carry your letter, which those who wish such murder not to remain hidden usually produce. Receive Caesar’s letter, father: let the man who recently avenged you instruct you himself. Receive Caesar’s writings, stronger than every argument. You recently used them for vengeance: use them now for safety. I bring these written characters as witnesses to my innocence. That right hand never deceived you; that right hand of Caesar placed the diadem upon you, it did not take it away. That mind of Caesar restored to you the kingdom you had cast aside. Caesar could have hated me first if he had found me like my brothers, but he examined me and pronounced me an interpreter of family devotion. Had I not been in Rome, Syllaeus would have won. To him I am condemned today; to him I, wretched man, pay the penalty. Remember, father, that I did not sail willingly. I already saw the pit of the conspirators being prepared for me, yet I preferred, father, that I should be endangered rather than you. Nor do I shudder at the danger to my life, but I grieve, father, to be endangered before you as though your enemy. Yet I am endangered if even Caesar’s testimonies are endangered before you: these, then, are the proofs I use in my defence. I do not appeal to Caesar as a man awaiting a hearing, but implore him as one already acquitted. If you think a trial must be held, here I am, father: I came to you after Caesar; I hastened to you from Caesar. If only I had never gone anywhere away from you! But you, father, unknowingly exposed me to dangers by ordering me to go. I am here, father, and I do not think the truth about your safety should be sought lightly from witnesses of lower standing. Let neither those who can fear torments nor those who can despise them prejudge the case. Scripture says, ‘Every human being is a liar.’ I offer the incorruptible testimonies of the elements. I come to you over seas and lands, never having suffered anything. Had I been guilty of attempting my father’s murder, I ought not to have escaped. Let heaven, which did not strike me with lightning, acquit me before you, father; the sea, which did not drown me; the earth, which did not swallow me. Through these I come to you safe, father, although even those who are not would-be murderers of their fathers often fail to escape them. The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram in its yawning chasm, yet they had not assailed the father who begot them. The earth suspended Absalom as he fled in the branches of its tree, lest he reach his father; had he reached him, he would have escaped. I have come to you and am still endangered. David avenged the son who would have murdered him because he could not save him. I do not ask to be avenged upon my enemies and false accusers by summoning them to torture. Let them escape the penalty for false accusation. I ask one thing, father: do not trust other people’s torments; inquire from me myself against myself. Hang up your accused: let the interrogation of truth proceed into my entrails, let the cords of interrogation descend into my body and its inner chambers, let the blood flow that is accustomed to cry out against the murder of a father, let fires be brought upon the guilty limbs. Why hesitate, father? If you spare me, you pronounce me innocent; if you refrain from torture, you acquit me of the crime. A man thought worthy of a simple death is no murderer of his father. Or if you spare me as your son and pity limbs begotten from yourself, those limbs are not yours that are instruments of cruelty.” Having said this, he ended his speech with much weeping and lamentable groaning, and with the greatest wailing moved Varus and everyone to pity. Herod alone was moved by no tears and himself refrained from weeping, implacable towards pardon, pressing for interrogation and seeking vengeance.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.1] At the king’s command Nicolaus followed Antipater’s speech, to answer his cunning skilfully and draw those who had been moved back from pity by turning upon Antipater the odium of his brothers’ murder. He argued that, if anyone was moved by pity, they ought to pity those who had been killed by his fraud and demanded vengeance. If they acquitted one man, the whole royal house would be brought into danger: brothers, relatives by marriage, parents, the king himself, whose life he had not spared. Turning therefore to the cunning of orators, as though in a kind of peroration he summoned from the underworld the souls of the slain to fill the court benches with their pitiful complaint: they had died innocent, weighed down by suborned witnesses, fabricated letters and fraudulent words. Their father had been deceived into trusting a son whom he did not think capable of lying about his brothers. Now this man offered himself for torture, although he had not believed his brothers’ torments; he had weighed them down with chains and bound them so that they could not attend the hearing. Sentence had been passed against absent men; they had been killed far away, lest their father pity them. No one would therefore be left if this man escaped, trained to pour poison for the murder of kin into his own kin’s entrails and change men’s minds. He had even roused Pheroras, who had always loved his brother Herod so greatly, to kill him in a deadly murder of kin.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.2] Nicolaus added very many other things to these to stir emotion. When he had finished his speech, Varus asked Antipater whether he wished to reply. He answered nothing except: “God is my witness that I have done no harm.” Then Varus ordered the poison to be brought forward and given to one of those already condemned to death. He drank it and died immediately. This was reported to Caesar, and Antipater was led away in chains at his father’s command.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.3] Yet he was not free from plots. For at that very time he was trying by deceit to endanger Salome. Antipater had sent letters composed in Salome’s name, full of insults against the king, and had ordered them to be conveyed through Antiphilus’s slave to Acme, the slave girl of Julia, who was Caesar’s wife, so that Acme would forward the letters delivered to her to the king. The fraud nearly succeeded in destroying the woman, but a letter from Acme to Antipater was found that exposed the deceit. It was written in this manner: “As you wished, I have written to your father and sent those letters, and I do not doubt that the king will rise to endanger his sister.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.4] You, having obtained the outcome you desired, repay the service.” When these letters were intercepted, the king was led to suspect that Alexander too had been assailed by letters fabricated by his brother with the same art, and, exasperated by excessive agitation, he contracted a grave illness. Seeing himself pressed by this danger, he named one of his sons, Antipas, as heir to his rule in his will, preferring him to his elder children Archelaus and Philip, since Antipater’s deceit and falsehoods had also made them suspect to their father. He bequeathed a thousand talents to Caesar, with gifts and presents added, and allotted five hundred to Caesar’s wife and children, freedmen and friends. Nor did he leave his sister Salome without a share in his gifts.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.5] The illness grew worse and became more severe with the passage of time, while the disabilities of feeble old age aggravated it daily. For he bore a body weighed down by no fewer than seventy years and afflicted also by frequent grief of mind, wounded by so many murders of kin, which it was the utmost misery either to have discovered in his sons or to have inflicted. Yet the illness burned incurably because Antipater, still alive, was feared.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.6] He also became more contemptible day by day: images of Caesar and likenesses of animals placed upon the temple contrary to the law were being torn down. The chief instigators were Judas and Matthias, teachers of the young, who told those conspiring with them that the time had come to avenge the wrong done by violation of the law. The sacrilegious man was paying the penalty: he thought that whatever power permitted was right, and, not bowed by religion but exalted by pride, had exercised his desire to do whatever he wished in the temple’s inner sanctuary as though it were a right. Although divine force was hastening vengeance, it nevertheless seemed noble that those consecrated to the temple should also demonstrate their freedom by defending the observances of their ancestral rite. No one ought to be deterred by fear of danger, since even to die for the ancestral law was a mark of immortality.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.7] They were the first to attempt to tear down the golden eagle fixed above the top of the gate. They were seized and brought before the king, and when asked whom they wished to obey in attempting so great a deed, they answered: “The ancestral law.” When he asked again what they trusted in, that they appeared so cheerful when summoned to the danger of death, they replied that they trusted in the rewards of devotion and dedication, the recompense for which would be paid to those who sought death for the ancestral rite.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.8] He could no longer bear the firmness of the reply. Raised above his illness by indignation, so that he overcame his weakness, he went out into the assembly of the people. There, bringing them before the people as guilty of sacrilege, he began to accuse them on the grounds that graver things were suspected from such deeds. Even if these were not proved, everyone nevertheless feared for himself and pleaded that the instigators who had been seized should pay with punishment and that proceedings should not be extended to the rest, lest the interrogation trouble more people, including those uninvolved and innocent. Thus entreated, he passed sentence upon those present, that they should be burnt alive.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.9] His infirmity increased from this, and the force of a graver illness consumed his whole body with various sufferings. His fever was violent, his itching intolerable; there were continual pains in his inner entrails without any interruption, and he was tormented by colic in his middle. Dropsy weighed down his feet, his private parts swarmed with worms, and spasms of the whole body, heavy breathing and deadly gasps were signs to anyone that he was being made to pay the penalty for the unjust murder of his kin and the sacrilegious sentence. Yet he did not yield in spirit, and in his desire to live struggled against his sufferings. The hot waters of Callirrhoe, which he sought across the Jordan, had done him no good. At Lake Asphaltites, healing for very many, he lay ill without any improvement. There, while he was being soothed with copious oil, his body relaxed and lost its strength; he turned up his eyes in the manner of the dying, his voice failed and he lost consciousness. But, roused by the noise of those crying out, he recovered.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.10] Wishing to return to his own lands, when he reached the region of the place called Jericho he devised a monstrous deed, driven by black bile and in a manner threatening death itself, so that peoples might be sent as funeral offerings to him. For he had already ordered the nobler men to be gathered from all Judaea, so that they should assemble from each village in one place. When his command was obeyed, he ordered them to be shut inside the hippodrome. He summoned Salome and her husband Alexas and entrusted to them a legacy of blood. He asserted that his death would bring joy to the peoples of the Jewish nation, and that he had therefore devised a way for his funeral commemoration to be celebrated most splendidly. He demanded of his family that, when he had breathed his last, they should immediately order all those confined there to be killed. Thus there would be no one in all Judaea or in any house for whom his death would be unmourned, since he would have left everyone an inheritance of mourning at home. As they bewailed the murder of their own kin, they would seem to be paying the king his funeral dues, and thus the joy of public wishes would be hindered by private griefs. Lest the wicked commands fail to be carried out, he ordered fifty drachmas to be given to each soldier, so that, with such a reward for crime set before them, the soldiers would not refuse the deadly service, offsetting the horror of carrying it out with the gain of the reward.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.11] He was already almost yielding to the torments of so great an infirmity, but he awaited the replies brought by the deadly embassy. It reported that Acme had been put to death in response to Herod’s complaint, and that Antipater too had been convicted of attempting his father’s murder and condemned to death. Yet, if his father wished to grant him the opportunity to flee, expelled from his homeland and kingdom, Caesar would give the order, passing sentence upon the crime but leaving the decision to family devotion. Nature had removed the necessity of killing kin. For, briefly revived by the power granted him to act as he wished, while he considered the manner of death, he was racked by pains and had desired to forestall the day of his own death. He therefore asked for an apple and a sword together, to take some refreshment by cutting the fruit with it as he was accustomed to do. Raising himself a little and leaning upon his elbow, he lifted his right hand, wishing to strike himself. But Achiabus rushed up and prevented the blow. The whole house rang with mourning, so that outside it was thought that Herod had died. Antipater exulted at the sound of lamentation and asked the guards to release him from his chains. But the man in charge of that duty not only refused the request but also reported it to the king. Exclaiming that he was being mocked while still alive, Herod sent assassins to kill Antipater and ordered him to be buried in Hyrcania after his death. He changed his will again and appointed Archelaus, the elder of the brothers, king, leaving Antipas as tetrarch.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.45.12] Thus he survived Antipater by five days and died, having held the kingdom for thirty-seven years from the time when the Romans ordered him to rule. From the time when he removed Antigonus, his rival for the kingdom, he spent thirty-four years in power. If only he had been as happy in life at home as in his public successes! For abroad prosperity favoured him so much that he was raised from private station to kingship and, after enjoying it for a great many years, died with his power intact, a difficult thing, leaving his children a succession to rule that he himself had not received from his own family. But within his house he was most unhappy and filled it with the bitter bloodshed and mourning of his own family. Yet he found no one to carry out his final cruelty. In this one act Salome effaced the disgrace of her earlier crimes: she released all those whom the king had ordered to be killed, saying that the king had afterwards repented of the deadly command, revoked his earlier instructions and ordered that they should all be sent home.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.46.1] Then, after the soldiers and the rest of the people had assembled in the amphitheatre, the king’s death was announced. Ptolemy came forward, a man who had remained one of the king’s most faithful friends to the very end. Bearing the ring he had drawn from the dead man’s finger, he praised the king and urged the people to remain calm. He opened a letter in which the king appealed to the soldiers most faithful to him and exhorted them to show goodwill and favour to his successor. The tablets of the will were also opened and read: Philip was named heir to the region of Trachonitis and neighbouring places, Antipas tetrarch, and Archelaus king, on condition, however, that his ring should be conveyed to Caesar and that the judgement and confirmation of all his arrangements should be reserved to him. His will was to be valid only if Caesar approved it. He ordered the remaining provisions to be observed according to his earlier wills.

paragraphs.rawText: [I.46.2] At once the soldiers acclaimed and applauded Archelaus. He was immediately surrounded by a ring of guards; they promised goodwill and pledged allegiance. After this the funeral was fittingly and magnificently arranged, with the whole display of royal wealth sent ahead and the splendour of a funeral procession. The bier was adorned entirely with gold and gems, its covering shone with purple dye, and the body was covered by a double purple robe fastened with a clasp glittering with precious stones. A diadem clung to his head with a golden crown above it, and a sceptre was in his right hand, so that one might think him alive. A band of Thracians went before him, and the Germans and Gauls, the royal guards, kept military order. Armed alike as though going out to war, they followed with sorrowful faces, as if grieving. The rest of the force went ahead in their usual equipment and accustomed dress, their commanders and centurions accompanying them. Fifty slaves and freedmen of the royal household also sprinkled spices, so that the whole road was fragrant with a sweet scent. The king’s sons and a very great crowd of relatives surrounded the bier. He was buried in Herodium, as he himself had commanded, two hundred stades from the place where his life had ended. Over so great a distance everyone escorted him with great ceremony, but not with equal affection from all. For fear had wrung out duty, not willing service; grief at least kept its judgement free within itself. Such was Herod’s end.
